newsitem.title: USA: Stocks, bonds tumble after jobless, NAPM reports.
newsitem.headline: Stocks, bonds tumble after jobless, NAPM reports.

text.p: Stocks and bonds tumbled on Friday as news of the lowest U.S. unemployment rate in 24 years and surprisingly robust manufacturing activity revived fears that inflation is creeping higher.

The Dow Jones industrial average plunged as much as 119.39 points, and was down 97.32 points, or 1.18 percent, at 8,125.29 at 2:40 p.m. EDT (1840 GMT). Decliners outnumbered advancers by a margin of 20 to 7 on moderate volume of nearly 350 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.

The Nasdaq index slipped 3.77 points, or 0.24 percent, to 1,590.04. The Standard & Poor's index of 500 stocks slid 12.53 to 941.76, and the American Stock Exchange dipped 4.28 points, or 0.66 percent, to 642.02.
In the bond market, the key 30-year Treasury fell two full points, pushing its yield to 6.44 percent from Thursday's 6.30 percent. Bond prices and yields move in opposite directions.
The dollar also took a hit, falling to 118.30 yen from late Thursday's 118.65 in New York. However, it rose to 1.8645 German marks from Thursday's 1.8385.

Stocks opened slightly higher even though the Labour Department released a stronger-than-expected employment report. But stocks joined the bond market in heading south after the National Association of Purchasing Management (NAPM) announced a surprisingly big jump in its index in July.
Analysts said the rosy economic data revived the financial community's lurking fears of inflation -- and the possibility of a rate hike by the Federal Reserve to head it off.

"We got low unemployment, jobs creation and a strong NAPM figure," said Robert Froelich, chief investment strategist at Kemper Funds. "The combination of these numbers, even if there was no sign of wage inflation, caused the stock market to think about the risk of higher rates."

The central bank's policy-setting Federal Open Market Committee raised the federal funds rate -- which banks charge each other for overnight loans -- a quarter percentage point to 5.50 percent on March 25, but left it unchanged at its last regular meeting on May 20. The committee's next meeting is scheduled for Aug. 19.

"The markets did not like all the information about the economy doing better," said Alfred Kugel, senior investment strategist at Alfred Kugel, Stein Roe & Farnham. "The increase in employment and improvement in manufacturing provided an excuse to sell."
Analysts said both bonds and stocks have been vulnerable to profit-taking, after staging a powerful advance in July.
"We're just giving back some of our recent gains," said Jim Benning, a trader at BT Brokerage.

In its much-anticipated monthly payroll survey, the Labour Department said the unemployment rate slid to a 24-year low of 4.8 percent. The agency said 316,000 new jobs were created outside the farm sector in July, compared with a revised 228,000 in June.
Economists on average had expected the report to show an unemployment rate of 4.9 percent and the creation of 193,000 new jobs in July, compared with 217,000 in June.

The National Association of Purchasing Management, meanwhile, said the economy continued to grow in July for the 75th month in a row. The association's index, which looks at nationwide production, new orders, prices and employment, rose to 58.6 percent in July from 55.7 percent in June.
